science-mind-b4458eafcb.headline: The AI Riemann hypothesis proof is almost certainly true, independent mathematicians attest
science-mind-b4458eafcb.fulltext:
Mathematicians are now almost certain the earth-shattering artificial-intelligence-created proof of the Riemann hypothesis is real.
This morning Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge claimed to have used the company’s Claude AI model to solve the Riemann problem, perhaps the most important open quandary in mathematics. The hypothesis, first posed in 1859 by mathematician Bernhard Riemann, suggests that a hidden pattern underlies the distribution of the prime numbers—those numbers that are divisible only by themselves and 1.

Now researchers have verified that the proof does seem to do what Alpöge claims. Alpöge initially checked the work by writing out the proof using the programming language Lean; if a Lean-coded proof compiles error-free, this is usually taken as confirmation that the logic and math in each step is correct.
But some questions remained. For instance, does the proof really address the Riemann hypothesis, or does it establish a subtly different point or idea? “The first question which one has to ask when judging a PDF which comes with some Lean code is: ‘what is the statement of the theorem in the Lean code, and does this correspond to the actual theorem statement,’” explained mathematician Kevin Buzzard of Imperial College London in a blog post.
A second question was whether the Lean code would successfully compile for other mathematicians. Independent researchers, including Andrew Sutherland, a mathematician at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, have now separately compiled Alpöge’s result in Lean without issues.
“The Lean proof has been compiled and independently rechecked by the Lean kernel with only the three standard axioms,” Sutherland says. “Honestly the chance that anything is fishy here is approximately zero.”
Researchers are still making sure that the proof does not include any hack, dodge or shortcut that changed the meaning of the initial hypothesis or any other mathematical rules or truths. This process, called a “comparator run,” typically takes a matter of hours.
“We still await a successful comparator run, which will check that (a) the code does not do anything nefarious like redefine the meaning of any of the symbols in the statement and (b) (assuming it’s run in paranoid mode) the code compiles with several independent kernels (so the code is not just exploiting an as yet unknown bug in Lean’s official kernel,” Buzzard wrote on an online chat server for the Lean community.

world-041a64125a.headline: Russian missiles land in Poland, as Europe holds military drills nearby
world-041a64125a.fulltext:
[Text below is Los Angeles Times's report of the same story — the original outlet blocks automated reading. The link still points to the original.]
Russian missiles land in Poland, as Europe held military drills nearby. NATO calls it a violation
- Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
- Poland’s prime minister called a Russian missile’s crash near the Ukrainian border an apparent provocation, as European troops rehearsed a possible postwar mission in Ukraine.
- NATO chief Mark Rutte called the missile’s entry into Polish airspace a grave violation; European leaders condemned the incident as authorities investigated. No injuries or damage were reported.
- The crash came amid a Russian barrage that killed at least eight people in Ukraine, disrupted power supplies and clouded U.S.-brokered efforts to end the war.
NOWA DEBA, Poland — Two Russian missiles and a suspected drone came down in Poland on Friday in what its prime minister said was probably a provocation timed to coincide with European military exercises in his country for a possible postwar mission in Ukraine.
The incidents occurred while Russia carried out a major nighttime bombardment of neighboring Ukraine. The development stoked tensions between Europe and Moscow just as the U.S. tries to add momentum to talks it is mediating on ending the war that began with Russia’s all-out invasion of Ukraine nearly five years ago.
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said it appeared that “we are dealing with an intentional provocation” by Russia.
There was no immediate comment from Moscow on the missiles and suspected drone, or on Friday’s drills.
One Russian missile is believed to have crashed around 22 miles from where the military exercises were taking place, officials said. A Kh-101 cruise missile went down roughly 30 miles from the Ukraine border, and what officials believe was likely a jet-powered drone hit about 20 miles from the border with Ukraine.
There were no immediate reports of injuries or damage.
European troops were taking part Friday in an unprecedented two-week military exercise that began Nov. 9 in southeastern Poland. Forces are preparing for a possible postwar mission in Ukraine aimed at helping to stabilize the country and rebuild its military.
European countries previously have expressed alarm at what they deem to be Russia’s attempts to destabilize the continent.
President Trump discussed the war at a summit in China on Thursday with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese leader Xi Jinping, according to his envoy Steve Witkoff. Another envoy, Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner, told European leaders that the United States believes Russia is “comfortable” with NATO-like security guarantees for postwar Ukraine, in what could be a step toward compromise.
Russia’s nighttime attack on Ukraine came hours after Putin vowed to retaliate for Ukrainian strikes this week on a bridge linking occupied Crimea with the Russian mainland. The bridge is vital to Moscow’s war effort.
NATO chief addresses a ‘grave violation’ by Russia
Images from closed-circuit cameras and a mobile phone in the region collected by Poland’s PAP news agency showed a large, loud explosion and a bright flash, apparently in a wooded area, in one of the crashes.
NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte called the development in Poland a “grave violation” of that country’s airspace. “This incident is clearly dangerous - a consequence of Russia’s ongoing war against Ukraine,” Rutte wrote on X.
Rutte is expected to go to Poland this weekend in response.
Under NATO’s collective security guarantee — Article 5 of its founding treaty — an attack on any ally should be considered an attack on all 32 members. It obliges members to provide support to that ally, most likely military backup, but does not limit them to that alone.
Article 5 is not triggered automatically. Ultimately, it is a political decision that all members must agree to. Poland also has the option to enact Article 4, which it did last year. This provides for emergency consultations only.
The development brought a chorus of European condemnation.
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham described it as “utterly unacceptable.” European Council President António Costa said that Russia “continues to spread (its) threats.” Germany’s Foreign Ministry called it “yet another example of Russia’s ongoing provocations.”
Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said the incident in Poland “demonstrates the threats posed by Russian aggression to the whole of Europe and the trans-Atlantic community.”
Later Friday, the chief of defense intelligence for the U.K. said he was confident that Russia “does not actively seek war with NATO.”
But, Lt. Gen. Matthew Jones said in a speech at a college in Cambridge, his greatest fear “is the risk of a significant miscalculation.”
“There are too many recent examples of reckless Russian behavior where, if the incident had been slightly different, the results could have been extremely serious,” said Jones, who did not directly mention the incidents in Poland.
Putin has said that Russia will not accept any European troops deployed to Ukraine after a prospective peace deal and will view them as legitimate targets.
Russian attacks batter Ukraine, killing at least 8
Overnight strikes killed at least eight Ukrainian civilians and wounded more than two dozen, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said. Russia fired more than 400 drones and more than 110 missiles, 27 of them ballistic and some carrying cluster warheads that scatter dozens of smaller bomblets across a wide area, he said.
The attack fit the pattern of Moscow’s heavy responses to eye-catching Ukrainian attacks, such as the ones this week on the Kerch Bridge, and added to uncertainty about the prospects for ongoing talks brokered by Washington.
Russia and Ukraine are still far apart on the possible terms for a peace deal.
Russia takes aim at Ukraine’s missile and drone plants
Russia’s Defense Ministry said the sites it hit Friday were linked to the Ukrainian military. It said it hit a facility where missiles are assembled, a plant making components for rocket fuel, and a facility where drones are assembled.
Ukraine said the deadly attacks also wounded more than a dozen people as apartment blocks, medical facilities, warehouses and three bridges took hits.
Russia’s nighttime barrage also extended its campaign to knock out Ukraine’s power grid ahead of winter. Strikes on power plants, substations and transmission lines forced Ukraine’s three operational nuclear power plants to reduce generation, bringing emergency outages in 11 regions, said Deputy Energy Minister Artem Nekrasov.
Ciobanu, Kullab, and Hatton write for the Associated Press. Hatton reported from Lisbon, Portugal and Kullab reported from Kyiv, Ukraine. AP writers Stefanie Dazio in Berlin, Jamey Keaten in Geneva, Lorne Cook in Brussels and Emma Burrows in Cambridge, England, contributed to this report.

ai-fd28116146.headline: Nasdaq erases all 2026 gains as AI sell-off dampens Anthropic’s second day of trading
ai-fd28116146.fulltext:
As Anthropic’s stock dropped during its second day of trading, the wider stock market dipped with it. On Friday, the Nasdaq Composite erased all its gains for 2026 and closed down 5% from its value on 1 January. The Dow Jones Industrial Average and S&P 500 closed in correction territory.
Anthropic’s record-breaking IPO failed to stem a global sell-off in AI-linked companies, and the tech-heavy Nasdaq erased some $4tn in market value this week, according to the Wall Street Journal.
Shares in the frontier AI company behind the Claude chatbot, which floated in the US on Thursday, fell by 9% on Friday, ceding most of the gains from the biggest initial public offering in history. They dropped to $88.30, towards the $83 level at which Anthropic priced its stock market debut.
Anthropic’s first two days as a listed company have been volatile. Its shares jumped by 17% on Thursday, after briefly surging by almost 40% when trading in the firm began.
US technology stocks followed Anthropic down on Friday, with the memory chipmaker SanDisk falling 14% and rival Micron down 12%. Nvidia fell 14%, eliminating hundreds of billions of dollars in market cap.
Neil Wilson, a UK investor strategist at Saxo, said there was “just relentless selling in tech”. He warned: “Anthropic shares tumbled to take an $85 handle as the post-IPO euphoria gives way to the reality of a steep sell-off across the tech and AI space that shows no sign of easing just yet.”
Global markets slumped on Friday too; Asian stock markets recorded their worst week since 2020, as shares in big chip companies fell. In Taiwan, stocks dropped 6.7% to hit their lowest point since mid-April, with the chip maker TSMC down about 6%.
The scale of the decline in Taiwan prompted the chair of its stock exchange to pledge to ensure the stable operation of capital markets, and reassure investors they should remain confident in the fundamentals of Taiwanese companies.
In Japan, the Nikkei index fell 5%, while South Korea’s tech-heavy Kospi index lost 5.5%. Shares in the tech investor SoftBank had their worst day in more than two years, down 14.5% in Tokyo, amid worries around its aggressive bets on AI.
European stock markets posted their biggest weekly loss since March 2025, with the pan-European Stoxx 600 dropping 1.9% on Friday. London’s blue-chip stock index hit a five-month low.
The sell-off followed losses on Wall Street on Thursday, where the main indices all fell by more than 2% on a day dominated by Anthropic’s IPO.
Chris Beauchamp, the chief market analyst at the investing and trading platform IG, said Anthropic could be “draining market liquidity”, as investors sell shares in other companies to raise funds to pay for stock in the newly floated AI firm.
“The slide from yesterday’s highs sends a message that there might be more at work here than investors realise, and while brokers are scrambling to buy more, that liquidity has to come from somewhere, and the other tech names may be the first ones to feel the pressure,” Beauchamp said.
Anthropic’s flotation has failed to ease worries around the AI trade, as investors increasingly question whether companies can deliver the returns necessary to justify the billions of dollars being poured into the AI buildout.
Daniela Hathorn, a senior market analyst at Capital.com, said: “The IPO demonstrated that demand for AI exposure remains strong, but it has not been enough to overcome concerns about elevated valuations, profitability and the sustainability of investment spending.
“The broader market mood has shifted from buying the dip towards questioning whether the correction has further to run. The weakness in equal-weighted indices suggests that selling pressure is no longer confined to a handful of technology giants, while Europe’s recent outperformance has also faded.”
Nvidia shares fell byafter California served the chip company with a subpoena as part of an investigation into whether its advanced semiconductors ended up in China.
Britain’s FTSE 100 share index dropped by 5.1% this week, its biggest weekly fall since the start of the Iran war.
Fears that US central bankers may raise interest rates to fight inflation have lifted the dollar to a 19-month high, and pushed down the gold price – with gold on track for its worst week since March.
Bitcoin hit its lowest level in four months, dropping below the $60,000 point for the first time since early July.

ai-9d24760f53.headline: Trump threatens ban on US firms building AI data centres overseas
ai-9d24760f53.fulltext:
Trump threatens ban on US firms building AI data centres overseas
Donald Trump has said he will ban US companies from building AI data centres overseas, threatening a "tremendous tax" for tech firms who do so.
"We're going to keep it all in this country," the US president said, while providing little detail on the potential policy he said others in his cabinet were hearing about for the first time.
Data centres were a central issue in the midterm elections earlier in November, with many Democratic candidates promising tougher regulation on their construction.
Tech giants including Meta and Google have entered agreements to build data centres overseas. It remains unclear how such a policy would be enforced if it was brought in.
"We're not going to allow our companies to build data centres outside of our country," Trump told reporters in a press briefing following his return from his trip to Asia.
"Because China will take all of them, and we're not allowing that to happen."
But whether that idea will become policy remains unclear.
"I don't know if that's a breaking story, but I haven't even said that to my people. But I'm telling them now, they're here," he said.
Trump floated the policy after saying the US was leading on data centre construction, and he would not allow China to beat the US when it came to AI - which he calls super intelligence, or SI.
It also follows an announcement earlier this week that would restrict the export of advanced computer chips and who can access the computing power provided by them.
Washington on Monday announced firms would require a licence to buy advanced chips, so US officials can monitor whether they are being used to serve Chinese companies or they are being smuggled into China.
The move will impact South East Asian countries that have invested heavily in data centres, as Chinese companies seek to rent computing power from overseas.
Data centres are crucial to the AI boom. The vast warehouse-style buildings house the advanced computer chips and servers that are needed to run AI programmes such as Claude and ChatGPT.
As of April there were about 3,000 data centres across the US, with another 1,500 in various stages of approval and construction, according to the Pew Research Centre.
Many of them are built in rural areas, and concerns about issues including noise pollution and energy consumption helped drive Democratic candidates promising tougher rules on data centre construction to wins on 3 November.
"You ought to take advantage of the data centres. Make them pay you, make them pay your community, but take advantage don't shut them off," Trump said.
"We have a lot of places that want them badly, and they're great places. They have energy and they have everything. They're tremendous assets."
Large tech firms - often called AI hyperscalers due to the size of their investments in AI - have also been branching out, and Canada has made moves to step in to offer itself as an alternative location for these sites, with less local pushback against projects so far.
Meta has already broken ground on a data centre in the province of Alberta, and Anthropic has signed a long-term agreement to lease a proposed data centre in Nova Scotia.
The BBC has reached out to Meta for comment on Trump's remarks.
In September Google announced a €13bn ($15bn: £11bn) investment in AI infrastructure in Finland, which included funding for three data centres.
Last month, building work for two of those centres was halted due to concerns over the clearance of more than 300 hectares of forest.
Trump called out the build in Finland specifically, saying his administration was "not allowing that to happen".
Google has been contacted for comment.

india-ab96d4d314.headline: Indian man sentenced to 19 years in prison for conspiring to kill Sikh separatist in New York
india-ab96d4d314.fulltext:
An Indian man was sentenced to more than 19 years in US prison on Friday after admitting to orchestrating a failed Indian government-backed plot to kill a Sikh separatist in New York City, in connection with what US and Canadian authorities have called a broader effort to target Indian dissidents.
Nikhil Gupta, 55, pleaded guilty in February to murder-for-hire, conspiracy to commit murder-for-hire and conspiracy to commit money laundering.
The US district judge Victor Marrero handed down the 235-month sentence at a hearing in a Manhattan federal court.
The discovery of alleged assassination plots against Sikh separatists in the US and Canada has tested relations with India, which has denied involvement in such plots.
Prosecutors accused Gupta of plotting with an Indian government official to kill Gurpatwant Singh Pannun, a dual US-Canadian citizen and lawyer at Sikhs for Justice in New York who has advocated for a sovereign Sikh state in northern India.
Gupta and the Indian government official, Vikash Yadav, arranged to have $15,000 in cash delivered to a purported hitman who was actually an undercover US law enforcement officer, court papers show.
Yadav is also charged in the case but is not in US custody. It is unclear whether he has hired a defense lawyer.
India’s government has dissociated itself from any plot against Pannun, saying it was against government policy.
Prosecutors with the Manhattan US attorney’s office had recommended a sentence of about 24 years in prison.
“This case cuts to the very core of American values,” prosecutor Ashley Nicolas said in court. “We don’t condone the use of violence to silence voices in this country, ever.”
Addressing the court on Friday, Gupta said he regretted straying from the non-violent example set by the Indian independence leader Mahatma Gandhi.
“I’m sorry to Mr Pannun, I’m sorry to the communities I hurt, I’m sorry to my own family,” Gupta said.
Pannun told the court that he was grateful to the US for prosecuting Gupta and said he would keep advocating for Sikh sovereignty.
“Self-determination for my people and my homeland, Punjab, is my lifetime goal,” he said.

india-3ba6ae21d7.headline: India's core infrastructure output hits new-series high of 10.9% in October
india-3ba6ae21d7.fulltext:
Output of key infrastructure industries rose 10.9 per cent in October, the fastest pace in the new series, driven by double-digit growth in coal, iron ore, electricity and cement production.According to the official data released by the Commerce and Industry Ministry on Friday, core sector production expanded by 0.8 per cent in October last year and 8.2 per cent in September 2026.Among segments, iron ore output rose by 26.4 per cent, electricity by 21.6 per cent, coal by 23.1 per cent, and cement by 15.4 per cent.However, production of natural gas (-7.6 per cent), crude oil (-4.1 per cent), and fertiliser (-12.2 per cent) fell during the month under review, the ministry said in the statement.The cumulative growth rate of core sectors during April-October 2026 was 6 per cent compared to 2.3 per cent in the corresponding period of the previous year, it added.The new series started in June. The base year has been shifted to 2022-23 and expanded from eight to nine sectors by adding iron ore.Production growth of refinery products and steel slowed to 3.4 per cent and 7.3 per cent, respectively, in October.Commenting on the data, Aditi Nayar, Chief Economist, ICRA Ltd, said while core output surged by 10.9 per cent in October 2026, the fastest pace in the new series, this was supported by a low base related to the shift in the festive calendar, with output having expanded by a marginal 0.8 per cent in the year-ago month.While both coal and electricity benefitted from a favourable base as well as elevated demand for the latter, the robust growth in cement and steel output in October 2026 indicates that construction activity has remained healthy, she said, adding that cement output has expanded by double digits for the fourth straight month in October."Given the higher number of holidays, we expect the core output growth to cool to mid-single digits in November 2026," Nayar added.

beyond-your-beat-914d0c809c.headline: 'Compensating with terror': Russia hits Ukraine with 400 drones, 110 missiles in one of war's largest att
beyond-your-beat-914d0c809c.fulltext:
Ukraine said Russia launched one of its biggest overnight attacks of the war on Friday, firing more than 400 attack drones and over 110 missiles, including 27 ballistic missiles, at several cities and regions.
Ukrainian president 
Volodymyr Zelenskyy
 described the barrage as one of the biggest attacks of the war, accusing Moscow of deliberately spacing out missile strikes to hamper rescue and recovery efforts. He said Russia fired missiles in successive waves, with gaps of 20 to 30 minutes, making it harder for emergency crews to extinguish fires, clear rubble and restore damaged infrastructure.
"There were people killed practically by the time specialists were inspecting the first damage to facilities and the Russians were launching follow-up strikes," Zelenskyy said in a post on social media.
The strikes hit several cities and regions, damaging energy facilities, transport infrastructure and residential buildings. Zelenskyy said the targets included bridges across the Dnipro river, railway facilities, substations and power lines linked to Ukraine's nuclear power plants and electricity connections with neighbouring European Union countries.
He said Russia also used missiles carrying cluster warheads, adding to the difficulty of responding to the attack. 
Emergency and repair work was underway across the country wherever security conditions allowed, with restoration deadlines set for affected regions.
Ukraine says it intercepts 79 cruise missiles
Ukraine's air defence forces shot down 79 cruise missiles during the overnight assault, Zelenskyy said, praising the performance of Ukrainian combat aircraft, including F-16s, Mirages and MiGs.
However, he said intercepting ballistic missiles remained significantly more difficult and depended on supplies from Ukraine's international partners.
Ukraine's forces also targeted three Russian ballistic missile launchers during the night. One was destroyed, while the impact of strikes on the other two was still being assessed, Zelenskyy said.
Zelenskyy called on Ukraine's partners to respond with concrete support rather than statements of solidarity, urging them to accelerate air defence deliveries.
He said he had instructed Ukraine's foreign ministry to contact countries preparing new air defence packages and separately discussed supplies of PAC-2 and PAC-3 missiles with the defence minister. Kyiv is also counting on the US Pentagon to release the deliveries it has been expecting.
Zelenskyy accused Russian president Vladimir Putin of ordering the attack to compensate for what he described as Moscow's diplomatic and military setbacks. He linked the strikes to Putin's recent meetings in China and said Russia was resorting to attacks on civilians amid weakening positions on the battlefield.
"Russia is trying to compensate for its military and diplomatic incapacity with precisely this kind of terror," he said.

agritech-838b4e2604.headline: As drought grips half of India, rural jobs collapse by 50%
agritech-838b4e2604.fulltext:
When the rains fail, a farming family’s first losses are not measured in tonnes of grain. They show up in smaller, quieter ways: a meal skipped, a child kept home to mind siblings while their mother searches for work, a goat sold at a distress price because there is no cash left. 
This year, millions of rural households across India are being forced into exactly these choices. And the one public programme designed to soften this blow has been doing less, not more.
The meteorological reality is stark. Between June and September 2026, the India Meteorological Department recorded 759.4 mm of rain against a long-period average of 868.6 mm—a shortfall of 12.6 per cent. By mid-September, the India Drought Monitor showed 52.5 per cent of the country’s land area as dry or in drought conditions, up from 38.9 per cent just a month earlier. With the World Meteorological Organization confirming that El Niño is firmly established and expected to last through February 2027, this stress will inevitably bleed into the rabi season and the summer ahead.
States are already sounding the alarm. Maharashtra has declared drought in 265 of its 358 tehsils, Andhra Pradesh in 388 mandals, and Karnataka has identified 177 of its 240 taluks as drought-hit. Back in June, the agriculture ministry had already flagged 111 high-priority districts where less than a quarter of farmland is irrigated—the very places where a failed monsoon hits hardest.
Yet, at the precise moment this safety net should have been expanding, it shrank. 
On July 1, 2026, just as the monsoon was faltering, the rural employment guarantee transitioned from MGNREGS to the new VB-Gram G framework. The resulting drop in support has been precipitous. Official figures show that in July 2026, the new framework generated just 7.67 crore person-days, compared to 15.33 crore under MGNREGS in July 2025—a collapse of nearly 50 per cent. The number of households receiving work fell by over 51 per cent. Over the July-to-September quarter, total person-days plummeted to 284 million, down from 418 million a year earlier. Average work per household dropped from 43.2 days in 2025-26 to a mere 17 days so far in 2026-27.
Economists rightly point out that part of this decline has administrative explanations: several states invoked the new law’s agricultural "pause period" in July, and Aadhaar-based biometric checks on the new platform successfully weeded out duplicate entries. These are valid reasons to read the data carefully. They are not, however, reasons to look away from the distress unfolding on the ground.
"Farmers are selling goats and sheep in distress as they have run out of cash and the VB-Gram G work is erratic," Sajal Kulkarni, who works with rainfed farmers in Marathwada and Vidarbha, recently noted. For a small farming household, livestock represents savings, insurance, and children’s nutrition rolled into one. Selling it during a drought is a catastrophic loss that takes years to rebuild.
In Rajsamand, Rajasthan, activists report that local officials were instructed not to accept work applications or issue muster rolls from mid-June onward during the administrative changeover. A worker who walks to the panchayat and is turned away does not appear in any statistic of unmet demand. That is the quietest, and most dangerous, part of this distress: work that was desperately needed but never officially recorded.
Women are bearing the brunt of this collapse. They accounted for 61.9 per cent of person-days under the scheme in 2026-27 up to late June. For many rural women, the job guarantee is the only paid work available close to home, and the only income they control directly. When that work dries up, so does a mother’s ability to buy pulses, school notebooks, or medicine. This is happening at a time when rural food inflation (6.13 per cent in August) is running higher than urban food inflation (5.6 per cent).
The employment guarantee has proven its worth in hard years before. A widely cited study by the NCAER and the University of Maryland credited the programme with driving at least a quarter of the decline in rural poverty after 2004-05. The lesson from that era is simple: in a bad year, the guarantee must expand on demand, quickly and close to home.
To course-correct, policymakers must take four practical steps immediately:
First, in every tehsil, mandal, and taluk declared drought-hit, the Centre and state governments must suspend any remaining "pause periods" and keep work open continuously through the rabi and summer months.  
Second, gram panchayats must be mandated to provide dated, signed receipts for every work application. Unmet demand must become visible, making the legal guarantee truly enforceable.  
Third, the work provided must be strategically chosen for drought-proofing: farm ponds, well recharge, desilting of tanks, and fodder plots. These are the exact assets that will buffer communities against the next dry year.  
Fourth, the drastic drop in person-days must be independently examined. Policymakers must separate genuine administrative de-duplication from the reality of workers who were simply turned away at the gate.
El Niño will eventually pass. But what remains in its wake are the irreversible choices a family made to survive: the animals sold, the high-interest loans taken, the months a daughter missed school. 
A job guarantee exists so that those choices are never forced. In a drought year, it should be the loudest programme in the village, not the quietest.
---
Dr. Ankita Raj is a Professor at Amity University, India, where she teaches and researches education, sustainability, and community well-being

ai-01449c61c8.headline: The most misunderstood graph in AI just got a major update
ai-01449c61c8.fulltext:
The most misunderstood graph in AI just got a major update
METR’s latest report finds that AI models are still improving at a rapid clip, but they show some weaknesses in tasks that require judgment.
A new report from the AI evaluation nonprofit METR finds that some AI capabilities are continuing to improve along an exponential trajectory—but it also indicates that models aren’t quite as good at tasks that require judgment as they are at coding.
The report is an update to the organization’s time horizon plot, which was widely shared—and widely misinterpreted, owing to the complexity of the measures it used. METR evaluated models by having them attempt a large suite of tasks, each of which had also been completed by humans. Each task’s difficulty was scored by how long it took the human testers to finish it—and then models were rated according to the length of the tasks that they could complete. That plot showed that AI systems were rapidly improving—every four months, the length of the tasks that frontier models could successfully complete doubled.
The updated plot adds more tasks—some that are estimated to take humans far longer than those in the original suite, and others that are more open-ended. One of the biggest questions in AI right now is the extent to which progress on “verifiable” tasks—where it’s possible to check automatically whether an AI system has succeeded or failed—carry over into tasks on which success or failure is harder to measure. We know how to teach neural networks how to do verifiable tasks: Researchers have the systems attempt one many times, strengthen the neural pathways that contribute to success, and weaken the pathways that contribute to failures. That’s why AI systems have become so good at coding and math, two domains where it’s possible to determine automatically whether a solution does or doesn’t work.
It’s much harder to apply this technique, known as reinforcement learning, to tasks where success is less well defined or takes longer to ascertain—such as choosing a new research direction. For the same reason, it’s tough to evaluate AI performance on these tasks, so METR’s original time horizon plot didn’t include any of them. But it’s precisely this type of task that will prove essential if AI systems are to automate research and development.
And AI research and development is an especially hot topic right now. Parts of the AI community are still reeling from a different, heavily redacted METR report from earlier this month, which claimed that AI might be speeding up the pace of AI progress at Anthropic by a factor of two. That report sparked fears that the company (which just had a blockbuster IPO) could soon achieve full recursive self-improvement, a regime in which AI systems autonomously design their own successors with no human involvement.
METR researchers have worked to make sure their new suite of tasks includes some of the fuzzier, judgment-laden ones that could be most relevant to AI research and development. In one task, they ask models to design new AI evaluations that METR could use in its research and then have human METR employees score the results. Even though the most advanced models are now better than almost every human at software engineering, here they fall short: Not one of the AI-designed evaluations was good enough for METR employees to consider it useful for their research.
In another task, models have to score philosophical arguments. This task is intended to capture the extent to which models can exercise good judgment—though METR writes in the report that employees disagree about how relevant the task is for automation of AI R&D. On this task, too, models fell short of human performance.
Though it’s difficult to score these new tasks—and even harder to determine what the scores mean—experts I spoke with appreciate that METR is incorporating new types of evaluations into its work. “We’re at the point where AI evaluations need to get more creative,” says Sayash Kapoor, a computer scientist and incoming professor at UC Berkeley. “Trying to push the envelope of the space of evaluations is a welcome change.”
Kapoor says he wasn’t surprised to see that models fall short of performance on more open-ended tasks, such as designing an AI evaluation—in a preprint from August, he and his collaborators reported that AI models are not yet able to reproduce human computer science research on their own. And in a Wednesday blog post, OpenAI reported that its models don’t do as well on the real-world tasks its employees assign them as they do on the easier, more verifiable tasks in METR’s original suite.
Still, people disagree about how to interpret current performance differences on easily verifiable and hard-to-verify tasks, Kapoor says. Though he thinks that research taste—the ability to choose promising questions, hypotheses, and experiments—will prove a major bottleneck in automating AI R&D, others contend that models trained on easy-to-verify tasks will eventually be able to successfully complete open-ended tasks as well. And progress on verifiable tasks doesn’t seem to be slowing down.
Even if the models do lag behind human performance on open-ended tasks right now, the new report suggests that they might be getting better. Some of the newest models, such as Opus 5.5, tend to achieve what METR calls “borderline above the bar” performance on the evaluation design tasks—not yet usable for METR's research, but promising. Just a year ago, every model was scoring in the “clearly below the bar” category.
But because these open-ended and judgment-heavy tasks are so tough to design and score, METR includes few of them in its report, and that makes it difficult to predict whether and how models might continue to progress in these areas. “The improvement we observe, I think that does tell us something for the current moment,” says Najoung Kim, a linguist and computer scientist at Boston University. “I’m not sure just yet how to think about how it would extrapolate.”
Matt Putz, a member of the technical staff at METR, says that predicting progress on these kinds of tasks is likely to remain difficult. “By their nature, hard-to-verify or judgment-laden tasks are much harder to study, and especially to quantify,” he said in an email. “Ultimately, I don’t think we’ll be able to establish trends as clean and robust as for the easy-to-specify [tasks].”
In general, METR is clearly butting up against the practical difficulties of testing AI performance on difficult and underspecified tasks—precisely the ones most relevant to automating AI R&D. METR’s time horizon plots score task difficulty by evaluating how long it would take a human to complete the task, and for the original plot they measured this quantity by actually having people try each task.
In the new report, however, the completion times are mostly estimates, because paying people for tasks that might take hundreds of hours, or that only a few experts are qualified to complete, is prohibitively expensive and time-consuming. Other tasks have more specific shortcomings—for example, for the philosophical argument task, just one person rated most of the arguments, and agents are judged by how well they agree with that particular individual. It’s possible that the scores would change if more experts were surveyed—but that, too, is time-consuming.
It’s still early days for evaluating models on tasks that are hard to validate or require judgment. And while the experts I spoke with see the inclusion of these tasks in METR’s newest time horizon plot as a clear step in the right direction, they agree that we are still far from achieving any definitive answers about whether, and how quickly, automated AI R&D might be coming. “This move toward open-ended tasks is promising,” Kapoor says. But, he adds, “there is just such a lot more to be done to actually get a fuller understanding.”

SEBI Explores India-Made AI Model for Stock Market Regulation, Says Chairman Tuhin Kanta Pandey
SEBI is studying a domestic AI system that could make regulatory tools cheaper and more accessible, particularly for smaller market intermediaries. A committee is examining the feasibility of joint development, data security and safeguards against inaccurate AI outputs. The regulator has not announced an implementation timeline.
The Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) is exploring the development of an India-made artificial intelligence (AI) model for the securities market, Chairman Tuhin Kanta Pandey said on Friday, November 20, 2026.
Speaking at the CII DFS Financing Summit in Mumbai, Pandey said a committee was examining whether a domestically governed SEBI AI model could be developed jointly with market participants. The proposed system is intended to make AI-based regulatory tools more affordable, secure and accessible, particularly for smaller regulated entities.
The regulator is considering whether the model could be developed as part of India's Digital Public Infrastructure (DPI). The committee is assessing the costs, opportunities and risks involved, along with the safeguards required before such a system can be introduced.
Pandey said the proposal remains at an initial stage, with consultations underway to determine whether a common AI model would be feasible. No development or implementation timeline has been announced.
The discussions come as SEBI expands the use of technology in market supervision and compliance monitoring. The regulator has already introduced AI-based tools to monitor advertisements issued by market intermediaries and examine compliance reports.
What Is SEBI Planning With Its AI Model?
SEBI is examining whether a securities market-specific AI system can be developed and governed domestically, with participation from regulated entities and other industry stakeholders.
The proposal is aimed at addressing the cost and accessibility of AI-based regulatory technology. Smaller intermediaries may not have the same resources as larger financial institutions to develop or maintain advanced AI systems.
A jointly developed model could provide a common technological foundation for regulatory applications, although SEBI has not specified how such a system would be operated or which entities would be involved.
The committee is also looking at the risks associated with AI, including the possibility of systems producing incorrect or misleading information, often referred to as AI hallucinations.
Pandey said appropriate safeguards would be necessary while examining the opportunities offered by the technology.
The regulator has not announced whether the proposed model would be used for surveillance, compliance reporting, risk assessment or other specific regulatory functions. These details would depend on the outcome of the feasibility assessment.
SEBI's Use of AI in Stock Market Regulation
SEBI's latest comments follow an earlier announcement in October, when Pandey said the regulator was considering a domestically governed AI model for the securities market.
At the time, he also outlined plans to strengthen AI risk management and supervisory practices through international regulatory cooperation.
The regulator is working on implementing the International Organization of Securities Commissions' supervisory toolkit for artificial intelligence. The initiative focuses on improving oversight of AI systems and managing the risks arising from their use in financial markets.
SEBI has separately been examining the responsible use of AI and machine learning by regulated entities. Its June 2025 consultation paper proposed principles covering accountability, governance and oversight of AI applications in the securities market.
The regulator's existing AI-based monitoring tools are already being used in areas such as advertisement scrutiny and compliance reporting. The proposed domestic model would be a separate initiative and remains under consideration.
For now, the committee's assessment will determine whether the model can be developed collaboratively and what safeguards would be needed. SEBI has not announced a formal rollout plan or a date for completing the exercise.

indian-startups-85de94c275.headline: Fintechs Bear The Brunt As Yes Bank Upgrades AI Safeguards
indian-startups-85de94c275.fulltext: Fintech platforms have emerged as an unlikely collateral damage as Yes Bank strengthens its defences against AI-driven cyberattacks. Sources told Inc42 that the cybersecurity upgrades at Yes Bank are disrupting workflows and delaying payouts at payment service providers. One fintech executive said that his platform was facing issues ever since Yes Bank sent an email, which noted that the bank was “implementing enhanced precautionary measures to safeguard” transactions. He was subsequently also informed that the bank was making changes to its banking APIs, which was delaying settlements. These changes, in turn, are impacting payment processing and settlement timelines for some businesses that rely on banking APIs to move funds. Another industry insider noted that the issues began to crop up after the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) issued directives to banks and other financial institutions to bolster their cybersecurity defences. According to the source quoted above, the RBI directions came after the recent cyberattack on the State Bank of India (SBI), referring to the data leak at the bank in October. The RBI is also said to have directed the banks and other financial institutions to ensure the funds of customers are not impacted by the growing wave of AI-assisted cyberattacks. Inc42 has reached out to Yes Bank for a comment on the matter. This story will be updated upon receiving their response. This comes as multiple Indian crypto exchanges continue to grapple with delays in processing withdrawals due to disruptions at its banking partners. Coinbase India had paused all withdrawals last week, before partially resuming payouts, citing an outage at its banking partner. CoinDCX, which has also been facing similar issues, claimed that upgrades at “most” of its partner banks was delaying the processing of INR withdrawals. Zebpay also said that payouts were taking longer than usual because of a technical disruption at its banking partner. Earlier yesterday, Razorpay also told its customers that it had to delay merchant settlements temporarily due to a technical issue at a partner bank. However, the IPO-bound unicorn later reinstated the service hours later. The development comes on the same day as CERT-In has issued an alarm over unauthorised transactions at technology service providers for banks and other financial institutions. Bank Vendors Under AI Attack In an advisory dated November 21, the cybersecurity watchdog flagged that malicious actors were using AI-driven cyberattacks to undertake unauthorised transactions at technology service providers, which handle government-linked payment processes, as well as platforms handling vendor payouts. CERT-In said that attackers altered business records or approval relationships and then used legitimate payment processes to approve fraudulent transactions. The watchdog did not elaborate on how much money of the proceeds had been funneled out. The cybersecurity agency said that the reported incidents involved cyberattackers misusing business applications and workflows, rather than direct exploitation of payment APIs alone. As per CERT-In, these attackers used trusted systems to process unauthorised transactions and exploited gaps in verification and reconciliation of changes to business records. CERT-In also noted that it has identified the following techniques used by attackers for perpetrating AI-assisted cyberattacks against fintech platforms: Automated reconnaissance to identify exposed systems, services and possible attack paths Rapid preparation and modification of exploits for known vulnerabilities, including through analysis of software updates and related technical information Use of multiple agents or automated workers to undertake reconnaissance, privilege discovery and other intrusion tasks in parallel Modification of scripts, requests and attack steps in response to errors, blocked attempts or information returned by targeted systems Use of valid credentials, legitimate administrative functions, trust relationships and external infrastructure to gain further access. As such, CERT-In also directed government entities to identify and restrict accounts and integrations that can approve payments or change payment-related records. Besides recommending undertaking independent certification for high-risk changes to payment records, it also called on the banks to reconcile critical business data maintained by service providers against authoritative records. It also called on the TSPS to restrict administrative accounts and control-plane privileges. CERT-In also directed fintechs to review unusual activity and monitor changes to payment-related business records.

indian-startups-d7daf7c9e7.headline: Anthropic’s Nasdaq Debut Sparks Buying Rush Among Indian Retail Investors
indian-startups-d7daf7c9e7.fulltext: Indian retail investors rushed to buy and trade Anthropic shares following its Nasdaq debut yesterday, with the Claude maker drawing substantial activity across overseas investing platforms Mudrex, INDmoney, and Vested. Anthropic accounted for around 40% of INDmoney’s international investment activity on its markets debut day, while its average order value was twice the platform’s average, according to the company. On Mudrex, around 35% of daily active users traded Anthropic shares. Trading activity was 20-30% higher than on a typical day, with the platform describing the response as comparable to that recorded during the SpaceX IPO. The average ticket size stood at ₹2,000-₹3,000, while several investors also set up systematic investment plans (SIPs) to build longer-term exposure, Mudrex said. “The response to Anthropic’s listing reflects the growing interest among Indian investors in accessing global assets, particularly companies at the forefront of emerging technologies such as AI,” said Prateek Gupta, head of business at Mudrex. Gupta added that investors are increasingly looking beyond domestic markets to diversify their portfolios and build long-term exposure to global assets. On Vested, Anthropic accounted for approximately 11% of total traded value and 9% of all trades during the session. It ranked second by traded value, behind AMD and ahead of NVIDIA, according to the platform. Activity was concentrated in the opening hours, with 84% of Anthropic trades on Vested placed within the first two hours. The average buy order stood at around $1,100. Buying Into The AI Boom For much of the AI boom, direct investments in companies such as Anthropic and OpenAI have been largely limited to VC firms, institutional investors, and wealthy individuals. Anthropic’s listing opens a route for retail investors to own shares in a company developing frontier AI. Overseas investing platforms facilitate access to US-listed companies for Indian investors, with eligible individuals able to invest through routes such as the Liberalised Remittance Scheme (LRS), subject to applicable regulatory and tax requirements. Indian retail investors using platforms such as Zerodha, INDmoney, and Vested can buy US stocks after listing but cannot subscribe directly to their IPOs through these platforms. Their entry price therefore depends on the market price when they buy, rather than the IPO offer price. Anthropic’s debut illustrated this price gap. Its shares opened at $111.50, a 34.3% premium to the $83 IPO price, before closing at $97.17 – up 17.1% from the issue price but down 12.9% from the opening price. The IPO was worth approximately $81.3 Bn, including shares sold by existing shareholders, and valued Anthropic at around $1.5 Tn at the offer price. The company also lined up $26 Bn in concurrent private placements involving technology partners, including Google, Microsoft, and NVIDIA. The debut came amid concerns about the cost of developing advanced AI systems and the returns companies can generate from infrastructure spending. Anthropic shares reportedly fell more than 3% in after-hours trading yesterday following reports that Apple was developing an autonomous AI agent, adding to competition from OpenAI and Meta. However, Anthropic shares fell around 10% in pre-market trading today amid a broader sell-off in AI-linked stocks, reversing part of yesterday’s debut gains. India’s AI Ambitions Beyond retail trading, the listing has reignited debate about India’s ability to build globally competitive AI companies. Anthropic’s $1.5 Tn valuation at the IPO price is equivalent to nearly 37% of India’s projected nominal GDP of $4.06 Tn for FY27, according to the IMF’s October estimates. The comparison illustrates scale, although a company’s valuation and an economy’s annual output measure different things. Veteran banker and Kotak Mahindra Bank founder Uday Kotak recently compared Anthropic’s valuation with the combined market capitalisation of India’s top 10 companies, questioning whether Indian businesses were undervalued or whether the country needed to catch up with the emerging technology economy. The debate comes amid rising investment in India’s AI ecosystem. Indian AI startups raised $676 Mn across 57 deals in H1 2026, more than 4X the funding recorded in the year-ago period. The sector attracted another $438 Mn across 35 deals in Q3, taking funding for the first nine months of the year to over $1.1 Bn. Building companies at Anthropic’s scale, however, will require sustained investment in research, computing infrastructure, technical talent, and product development.

india-deep-tech-8898659a03.fulltext:
Andhra Pradesh
AP raises semiconductor incentives, offers up to 80% support for silicon fabs
The revised policy extends support to chip design, machinery, materials, research and talent development, alongside manufacturing incentives.
The Andhra Pradesh government has amended its Semiconductor and Display Fab Policy 4.0 to align it with the second phase of the India Semiconductor Mission (ISM 2.0), offering state incentives that match Union support for several project categories.
The amendment, notified through G.O.Ms.No.87 on November 16, provides combined Union and State incentives of up to 80% of eligible capital costs for silicon fabrication projects, with each government contributing 40%.
Compound semiconductor, photonics, sensor, discrete semiconductor and display fabrication projects, as well as advanced packaging units, will be eligible for combined support of up to 70%. Legacy packaging units can receive up to 50%, according to the policy details.
For assembly, testing, marking and packaging (ATMP) and outsourced semiconductor assembly and test (OSAT) facilities, Andhra Pradesh will match 100% of the Centre’s capital support. The state will also provide a deployment-linked incentive of 4.5% of net sales, in addition to the Union’s 9%, taking the combined incentive to 13.5%. This support will be capped at Rs 45 crore per application and Rs 180 crore per company.
For semiconductor machinery and materials projects, the state will provide 18% of eligible capital costs on top of the Union’s 30%, bringing the combined support to 48%, in addition to the Union’s production-linked incentive. Research and development and talent projects will receive state support of 25% of eligible project costs, with combined Union and State assistance capped at 75%.
IT Minister Nara Lokesh said the amended policy covers all 10 categories under ISM 2.0, across six pillars: design, machinery and materials, fabrication, packaging, research and development, and talent.
The state is also planning a 5,000-acre AP Semiconductor Park in Tirupati to host manufacturers and suppliers across the value chain. The proposed park would provide developed land, shared cleanrooms, reliable high-voltage power, ultrapure water, gas supplies, effluent treatment and recycling, testing laboratories, logistics facilities, and research and training centres.
A public-private company with an investor-led board would operate the park, with up to three government nominees. The government also plans to establish an AP Semiconductor Growth and Innovation Council as a single point of contact for investors, alongside an Oversight Council chaired by the Chief Minister and a CEO-led Apex Committee.
The AP Semiconductor Research and Innovation Centre is proposed as a not-for-profit organisation with independent professional management. It will initially operate at IIT Tirupati before moving to the park, with photonics as its first area of focus.
The amended policy will remain in force for five years or until it is replaced by a new policy. Existing benefits will be protected, while separate operating guidelines will set out eligibility, appraisal and disbursement procedures.

india-6b46effd97.source: India Latest News: Top National Headlines Today & Breaking News | The Hindu
india-6b46effd97.fulltext:
The Congress party on Friday said it favoured resolving the issue of delimitation through consultations with all political parties, but accused the government of making no effort to engage the Opposition on the matter.
Congress general secretary Jairam Ramesh said the party’s position was guided by a four-point formula: retaining the existing strength of 543 seats in the Lok Sabha; maintaining the present State-wise distribution of seats; reserving one-third (182) of the existing seats for women; and imposing a 25-year freeze on all three arrangements.
Mr. Ramesh said the need for an early consensus on the issue had become more pressing in view of of the fact that Article 82 of the Constitution will come into force and delimitation would be held once the results of the ongoing Census exercise are out early next year.
This could be unfavourable to some southern states – which have made progress in population control – and hence not feasible, he added.
Mr. Ramesh said the Congress was not opposed to delimitation as such, but believed that the exercise should not place any State at a disadvantage.
The Congress leader claimed that all parties in the INDIA bloc, including the Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam (DMK) and the Nationalist Congress Party (Sharadchandra Pawar), were on the same page on the four-point formula.
The DMK, he said, was also party to a resolution opposing any change in the number of Lok Sabha seats and seeking safeguards to ensure that Tamil Nadu was not disadvantaged by delimitation.
The Congress leader said seeking consultation was necessary because the government had not initiated any meaningful engagement with the Opposition.
He claimed that as per his information, the government has not shared a concrete proposal on delimitation even with constituents of the National Democratic Alliance.
The Congress wanted the matter to be discussed with all political parties and stakeholders to arrive at a consensus, Mr. Ramesh added.
The Monsoon session of Parliament has remained unprorogued since both Houses were adjourned sine die on August 13.
The decision has fuelled speculation about the possibility of the government convening Parliament at short notice to consider the proposed constitutional changes linked to women’s reservation and delimitation.
An extended or special sitting within the same session requires a minimum notice of two days, while convening a fresh session requires at least 14 days’ notice.
Speculation also continues over the timing of the winter session. Parliament has not held a winter session on four occasions: in 1975, 1979, 1984 and 2020.

Mr. Malik, who arrived here in the early hours of Friday (November 20, 2026), attended the opening day of the three-day forum in the evening. The event, being hosted by India at the historic Purana Quila, was inaugurated by Prime Minister Narendra Modi.
India had announced on October 28 that invitations had been extended to all SCO members, including Pakistan, in keeping with established practice.
It was perhaps the first time New Delhi had invited a Pakistani minister to attend an event in India since the May 7-10 military hostilities last year following Operation Sindoor.
Pakistan had announced on November 14 that its Climate Change Minister Malik would participate in the forum.
At his bi-weekly media briefing, Ministry of External Affairs (MEA) spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal was asked how New Delhi viewed Mr. Malik's participation in the India-hosted forum, given that he does not hold the culture portfolio and had reportedly made comments on the IWT.
"As far as IWT is concerned, we have made our position very clear, and that is where it remains. There is absolutely no change," Mr. Jaiswal said.
India suspended the treaty in 2025 as one of the punitive measures against Pakistan after the April 22 Pahalgam terror attack last year that claimed 26 lives.
Mr. Malik's participation in the forum is being seen by some experts as an opportunity in a multilateral framework that may help improve ties between the two neighbours.
Interacting with reporters on the sidelines of the forum, Mr. Malik, when asked about the role of culture in fostering better ties between India and Pakistan, said, "Culture has a very key role to play".
Hours before the inauguration, the MEA on Friday (November 20, 2026) said the forum was a "multilateral event within the SCO framework", for which invitations had been extended to all members of the grouping, including Pakistan.
"India is hosting the 1st SCO Civilisation Dialogue on 20-22 November 2026, in New Delhi. This is a multilateral event within the SCO framework, for which invitations have been extended to all members of the SCO, including Pakistan," the MEA said in a post on X.
"Observers and Dialogue Partners of the SCO have also been invited to attend the Dialogue, which will be inaugurated this evening by the Hon’ble Prime Minister," it said.
The event is being hosted by the Ministry of Culture and the MEA.
The SCO was founded at a summit in Shanghai in 2001 by the presidents of Russia, China, the Kyrgyz Republic, Kazakhstan, Tajikistan and Uzbekistan. India and Pakistan became its permanent members in 2017.

world-2c3757b089.headline: California investigates Nvidia over whether chip exports ended up in China
world-2c3757b089.fulltext:
California has served an investigative subpoena on Nvidia after a scandal that prompted the departure of co-founder and longtime chief executive Jensen Huang.
Rob Bonta, the US state’s attorney general, issued the subpoena as part of an investigation into whether exports of the California-based company’s advanced semiconductor chips ended up in China, contravening US restrictions.
“The conduct of Nvidia and its former chief executive raises bright red flags, including about the ways in which the company may have misled investors,” said Bonta.
“Nvidia is in a messy, transnational situation but the underlying principle of our corporate securities law is clear: companies cannot mislead their investors.”
The subpoena, issued on Thursday, followed Huang’s resignation a week ago after it emerged he had multiple affairs, including one with Alice Huang, a suspected Chinese spy.
Alice Huang, who is not related, is associated with Singapore-based Megaspeed, which has bought nearly $5bn (£3.8bn) of Nvidia chips and hardware in recent years, and is being investigated for possibly diverting advanced restricted chips to China.
Megaspeed has said it is a “legitimate and lawful” business, and that Huang left the company late last year.
Bonta said the investigation would also look at whether the former Nvidia chief’s actions resulted in confidential information being passed to China.
“My office is investigating whether Nvidia or Jensen Huang’s actions resulted in China obtaining advanced chips or confidential information,” he said. “And if Nvidia misled investors and the public about this risk, in violation of the law.”
Nvidia’s shares are down by a fifth since Huang admitted the extramarital affair, hitting a one-year low at the close of trading on Thursday, and wiping almost $1tn off its market value.
Earlier this week, Harvey Jones, Nvidia’s chair, said the company had no intention of reinstating Huang after the former CEO said he would be “honoured” to return. Elon Musk and a host of tech bosses had campaigned for Nvidia to bring him back.
Huang is due to testify before several congressional committees over the potential breach of national security on 1 December.
Shares in rival chipmaker AMD closed down almost 8% on Thursday after the publication of reports connected to short seller Hunterbrook warning about its links to China and the “circular financing” of customers.
The company, which has been targeted amid the Nvidia scandal, is looking at a further fall of more than 5% in pre-market trading.
Hunterbrook Media published allegations on the use of AMD’s software by a Chinese server maker blacklisted by the US. Sister publication, The Bear Cave newsletter, alleged that AMD’s use of datacentre lease guarantees and backstops for unsold cloud computing capacity could leave it exposed to a pullback in AI spending.
AMD said the reports’ claims “misrepresent AMD’s business practices and relationships”.
“AMD complies with applicable US export control laws and regulations and maintains rigorous processes to ensure compliance across our global operations,” the company said. “We remain focused on serving our customers and upholding the highest standards of integrity.”
AMD’s share price has more than doubled so far this year, giving the company a market capitalisation of more than $800m.

longform-cf67f8030c.headline: Is This the Hidden Cause of Allergies?
longform-cf67f8030c.fulltext:
Allergies are on the rise. According to government statistics, cases of eczema, hay fever, and food allergies have been steadily climbing in the United States over the past few decades, leaving researchers puzzled. A slew of hypotheses for the increase have been offered—from too much hygiene to not enough gut microbes. Now, a new study published in the journal Allergy suggests our understanding of the illnesses may be flawed from the beginning.
Allergies have traditionally been understood as an exaggerated response from an oversensitive immune system. A harmless allergen triggers a cascade of immune activity causing sneezes, inflammation, and in extreme cases even death. On a tissue level, part of the damage done by allergies has been to epithelial barrier cells lining the gut, skin, airways, and more. But what if we have things backwards?
Read more: “The Perils of Early Springtime”
“For 60 years, we’ve taught that allergies start with the immune system and the barrier breaks as a consequence, but our work suggests it may be the other way around,” study author Peter K. Smith said in a statement. “Allergy diseases, which now affect up to one in three children, may start one step earlier as a power failure in the mitochondria of the epithelial cells which form the body’s barrier surfaces.”
Smith and a team developed the hypothesis after analyzing public datasets from more than 110 case-control cohorts, which included over 3,700 allergy patients, focusing on the genes that were transcribed in barrier cells. They found that genes responsible for clearing damaged mitochondria in the cells were less active in those suffering from allergies.
According to the team, this mitochondrial failure may represent the first domino to fall, which means it could be the primary cause of many allergies. Under their model, a leaky barrier stemming from dysfunctional mitochondria kickstarts the rest of the immune cascade, rather than vice versa. “The barrier cell can’t meet the energy and stress demands of the modern environment so it raises the alarm too easily, and the immune events we recognize as an allergy, follow,” Smith explained.
The strongest evidence for the theory was among eosinophilic esophagitis patients, with all cohorts studied showing diminished mitochondria-clearing transcription activity. The same pattern was present in eczema patients—even among skin cells that weren’t inflamed. However, there were still some inconsistencies. Those with hay fever only showed a partially diminished capacity to clear damaged mitochondria, and the pattern was completely absent from those with asthma and nasal polyps.
In other words, there’s more work to be done. But the findings may give researchers a new perspective into a set of diseases that have been stubbornly rising. Or as Smith put it, “This is not a cure but is something we have never had before—a logical starting point.”

Russian missiles land in Poland, as Europe held military drills nearby. NATO calls it a violation
- Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
- Poland’s prime minister called a Russian missile’s crash near the Ukrainian border an apparent provocation, as European troops rehearsed a possible postwar mission in Ukraine.
- NATO chief Mark Rutte called the missile’s entry into Polish airspace a grave violation; European leaders condemned the incident as authorities investigated. No injuries or damage were reported.
- The crash came amid a Russian barrage that killed at least eight people in Ukraine, disrupted power supplies and clouded U.S.-brokered efforts to end the war.
NOWA DEBA, Poland — Two Russian missiles and a suspected drone came down in Poland on Friday in what its prime minister said was probably a provocation timed to coincide with European military exercises in his country for a possible postwar mission in Ukraine.
The incidents occurred while Russia carried out a major nighttime bombardment of neighboring Ukraine. The development stoked tensions between Europe and Moscow just as the U.S. tries to add momentum to talks it is mediating on ending the war that began with Russia’s all-out invasion of Ukraine nearly five years ago.
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said it appeared that “we are dealing with an intentional provocation” by Russia.
There was no immediate comment from Moscow on the missiles and suspected drone, or on Friday’s drills.
One Russian missile is believed to have crashed around 22 miles from where the military exercises were taking place, officials said. A Kh-101 cruise missile went down roughly 30 miles from the Ukraine border, and what officials believe was likely a jet-powered drone hit about 20 miles from the border with Ukraine.
There were no immediate reports of injuries or damage.
European troops were taking part Friday in an unprecedented two-week military exercise that began Nov. 9 in southeastern Poland. Forces are preparing for a possible postwar mission in Ukraine aimed at helping to stabilize the country and rebuild its military.
European countries previously have expressed alarm at what they deem to be Russia’s attempts to destabilize the continent.
President Trump discussed the war at a summit in China on Thursday with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese leader Xi Jinping, according to his envoy Steve Witkoff. Another envoy, Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner, told European leaders that the United States believes Russia is “comfortable” with NATO-like security guarantees for postwar Ukraine, in what could be a step toward compromise.
Russia’s nighttime attack on Ukraine came hours after Putin vowed to retaliate for Ukrainian strikes this week on a bridge linking occupied Crimea with the Russian mainland. The bridge is vital to Moscow’s war effort.
NATO chief addresses a ‘grave violation’ by Russia
Images from closed-circuit cameras and a mobile phone in the region collected by Poland’s PAP news agency showed a large, loud explosion and a bright flash, apparently in a wooded area, in one of the crashes.
NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte called the development in Poland a “grave violation” of that country’s airspace. “This incident is clearly dangerous - a consequence of Russia’s ongoing war against Ukraine,” Rutte wrote on X.
Rutte is expected to go to Poland this weekend in response.
Under NATO’s collective security guarantee — Article 5 of its founding treaty — an attack on any ally should be considered an attack on all 32 members. It obliges members to provide support to that ally, most likely military backup, but does not limit them to that alone.
Article 5 is not triggered automatically. Ultimately, it is a political decision that all members must agree to. Poland also has the option to enact Article 4, which it did last year. This provides for emergency consultations only.
The development brought a chorus of European condemnation.
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham described it as “utterly unacceptable.” European Council President António Costa said that Russia “continues to spread (its) threats.” Germany’s Foreign Ministry called it “yet another example of Russia’s ongoing provocations.”
Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said the incident in Poland “demonstrates the threats posed by Russian aggression to the whole of Europe and the trans-Atlantic community.”
Later Friday, the chief of defense intelligence for the U.K. said he was confident that Russia “does not actively seek war with NATO.”
But, Lt. Gen. Matthew Jones said in a speech at a college in Cambridge, his greatest fear “is the risk of a significant miscalculation.”
“There are too many recent examples of reckless Russian behavior where, if the incident had been slightly different, the results could have been extremely serious,” said Jones, who did not directly mention the incidents in Poland.
Putin has said that Russia will not accept any European troops deployed to Ukraine after a prospective peace deal and will view them as legitimate targets.
Russian attacks batter Ukraine, killing at least 8
Overnight strikes killed at least eight Ukrainian civilians and wounded more than two dozen, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said. Russia fired more than 400 drones and more than 110 missiles, 27 of them ballistic and some carrying cluster warheads that scatter dozens of smaller bomblets across a wide area, he said.
The attack fit the pattern of Moscow’s heavy responses to eye-catching Ukrainian attacks, such as the ones this week on the Kerch Bridge, and added to uncertainty about the prospects for ongoing talks brokered by Washington.
Russia and Ukraine are still far apart on the possible terms for a peace deal.
Russia takes aim at Ukraine’s missile and drone plants
Russia’s Defense Ministry said the sites it hit Friday were linked to the Ukrainian military. It said it hit a facility where missiles are assembled, a plant making components for rocket fuel, and a facility where drones are assembled.
Ukraine said the deadly attacks also wounded more than a dozen people as apartment blocks, medical facilities, warehouses and three bridges took hits.
Russia’s nighttime barrage also extended its campaign to knock out Ukraine’s power grid ahead of winter. Strikes on power plants, substations and transmission lines forced Ukraine’s three operational nuclear power plants to reduce generation, bringing emergency outages in 11 regions, said Deputy Energy Minister Artem Nekrasov.
Ciobanu, Kullab, and Hatton write for the Associated Press. Hatton reported from Lisbon, Portugal and Kullab reported from Kyiv, Ukraine. AP writers Stefanie Dazio in Berlin, Jamey Keaten in Geneva, Lorne Cook in Brussels and Emma Burrows in Cambridge, England, contributed to this report.

global-economics-fd28116146.headline: Nasdaq erases all 2026 gains as AI sell-off dampens Anthropic’s second day of trading
global-economics-fd28116146.fulltext:
As Anthropic’s stock dropped during its second day of trading, the wider stock market dipped with it. On Friday, the Nasdaq Composite erased all its gains for 2026 and closed down 5% from its value on 1 January. The Dow Jones Industrial Average and S&P 500 closed in correction territory.
Anthropic’s record-breaking IPO failed to stem a global sell-off in AI-linked companies, and the tech-heavy Nasdaq erased some $4tn in market value this week, according to the Wall Street Journal.
Shares in the frontier AI company behind the Claude chatbot, which floated in the US on Thursday, fell by 9% on Friday, ceding most of the gains from the biggest initial public offering in history. They dropped to $88.30, towards the $83 level at which Anthropic priced its stock market debut.
Anthropic’s first two days as a listed company have been volatile. Its shares jumped by 17% on Thursday, after briefly surging by almost 40% when trading in the firm began.
US technology stocks followed Anthropic down on Friday, with the memory chipmaker SanDisk falling 14% and rival Micron down 12%. Nvidia fell 14%, eliminating hundreds of billions of dollars in market cap.
Neil Wilson, a UK investor strategist at Saxo, said there was “just relentless selling in tech”. He warned: “Anthropic shares tumbled to take an $85 handle as the post-IPO euphoria gives way to the reality of a steep sell-off across the tech and AI space that shows no sign of easing just yet.”
Global markets slumped on Friday too; Asian stock markets recorded their worst week since 2020, as shares in big chip companies fell. In Taiwan, stocks dropped 6.7% to hit their lowest point since mid-April, with the chip maker TSMC down about 6%.
The scale of the decline in Taiwan prompted the chair of its stock exchange to pledge to ensure the stable operation of capital markets, and reassure investors they should remain confident in the fundamentals of Taiwanese companies.
In Japan, the Nikkei index fell 5%, while South Korea’s tech-heavy Kospi index lost 5.5%. Shares in the tech investor SoftBank had their worst day in more than two years, down 14.5% in Tokyo, amid worries around its aggressive bets on AI.
European stock markets posted their biggest weekly loss since March 2025, with the pan-European Stoxx 600 dropping 1.9% on Friday. London’s blue-chip stock index hit a five-month low.
The sell-off followed losses on Wall Street on Thursday, where the main indices all fell by more than 2% on a day dominated by Anthropic’s IPO.
Chris Beauchamp, the chief market analyst at the investing and trading platform IG, said Anthropic could be “draining market liquidity”, as investors sell shares in other companies to raise funds to pay for stock in the newly floated AI firm.
“The slide from yesterday’s highs sends a message that there might be more at work here than investors realise, and while brokers are scrambling to buy more, that liquidity has to come from somewhere, and the other tech names may be the first ones to feel the pressure,” Beauchamp said.
Anthropic’s flotation has failed to ease worries around the AI trade, as investors increasingly question whether companies can deliver the returns necessary to justify the billions of dollars being poured into the AI buildout.
Daniela Hathorn, a senior market analyst at Capital.com, said: “The IPO demonstrated that demand for AI exposure remains strong, but it has not been enough to overcome concerns about elevated valuations, profitability and the sustainability of investment spending.
“The broader market mood has shifted from buying the dip towards questioning whether the correction has further to run. The weakness in equal-weighted indices suggests that selling pressure is no longer confined to a handful of technology giants, while Europe’s recent outperformance has also faded.”
Nvidia shares fell byafter California served the chip company with a subpoena as part of an investigation into whether its advanced semiconductors ended up in China.
Britain’s FTSE 100 share index dropped by 5.1% this week, its biggest weekly fall since the start of the Iran war.
Fears that US central bankers may raise interest rates to fight inflation have lifted the dollar to a 19-month high, and pushed down the gold price – with gold on track for its worst week since March.
Bitcoin hit its lowest level in four months, dropping below the $60,000 point for the first time since early July.
