world-36fb31620a.fulltext:
Trump threatens ban on US firms building AI data centres overseas
- Published
Donald Trump has said he will ban US companies from building AI data centres overseas, threatening a "tremendous tax" for tech firms who do so.
"We're going to keep it all in this country," the US president said, while providing little detail on the potential policy he said others in his cabinet were hearing about for the first time.
Data centres were a central issue in the midterm elections earlier in November, with many Democratic candidates promising tougher regulation on their construction.
Tech giants including Meta and Google have entered agreements to build data centres overseas. It remains unclear how such a policy would be enforced if it was brought in.
"We're not going to allow our companies to build data centres outside of our country," Trump told reporters in a press briefing following his return from his trip to Asia.
"Because China will take all of them, and we're not allowing that to happen."
But whether that idea will become policy remains unclear.
"I don't know if that's a breaking story, but I haven't even said that to my people. But I'm telling them now, they're here," he said.
Trump floated the policy after saying the US was leading on data centre construction, and he would not allow China to beat the US when it came to AI - which he calls super intelligence, or SI.
It also follows an announcement earlier this week that would restrict the export of advanced computer chips and who can access the computing power provided by them.
Washington on Monday announced firms would require a licence to buy advanced chips, so US officials can monitor whether they are being used to serve Chinese companies or they are being smuggled into China.
The move will impact South East Asian countries that have invested heavily in data centres, as Chinese companies seek to rent computing power from overseas.
- Why Canada is embracing AI data centres while the US pushes back 
  - Published1 day ago
Data centres are crucial to the AI boom. The vast warehouse-style buildings house the advanced computer chips and servers that are needed to run AI programmes such as Claude and ChatGPT.
As of April there were about 3,000 data centres across the US, with another 1,500 in various stages of approval and construction, according to the Pew Research Centre.
Many of them are built in rural areas, and concerns about issues including noise pollution and energy consumption helped drive Democratic candidates promising tougher rules on data centre construction to wins on 3 November.
"You ought to take advantage of the data centres. Make them pay you, make them pay your community, but take advantage don't shut them off," Trump said.
"We have a lot of places that want them badly, and they're great places. They have energy and they have everything. They're tremendous assets."
Large tech firms - often called AI hyperscalers due to the size of their investments in AI - have also been branching out, and Canada has made moves to step in to offer itself as an alternative location for these sites, with less local pushback against projects so far.
Meta has already broken ground on a data centre, external in the province of Alberta, and Anthropic has signed a long-term agreement to lease a proposed data centre in Nova Scotia.
The BBC has reached out to Meta for comment on Trump's remarks.
In September Google announced a €13bn ($15bn: £11bn) investment in AI infrastructure in Finland, which included funding for three data centres.
Last month, building work for two of those centres was halted due to concerns over the clearance of more than 300 hectares of forest.
Trump called out the build in Finland specifically, saying his administration was "not allowing that to happen".
Google has been contacted for comment.

  November 21, 2026 / 04:01 IST  
US President Donald Trump has threatened to impose a "tremendous tax" on American companies that build data centres outside the country, saying the move is aimed at strengthening the US artificial intelligence industry against competition from China.
"We're not going to allow our companies to build data centers outside of our country," Trump said at a White House news conference on Friday following his trip to Asia. He warned that companies setting up such facilities overseas would face heavy taxation.
Data centres are a crucial part of the AI ecosystem, providing the computing infrastructure required to train and operate increasingly sophisticated AI models. Trump's proposed move could have significant implications for American technology companies and the global expansion of AI infrastructure.
Major US data centre operators, including Equinix and Digital Realty, already develop and run facilities in overseas markets.
Companies typically establish data centres closer to their users to reduce latency, particularly for services that require real-time processing, such as payment transactions. Moving large volumes of data across long distances can also increase operating costs.
Trump has repeatedly pushed for more data centre construction within the US, although such projects have faced opposition from local communities. Concerns over rising electricity consumption, pressure on power grids and higher utility bills have fuelled resistance to new facilities across the country.
US tightens restrictions on AI chip exports
Trump's comments come amid broader US efforts to prevent China from accessing advanced artificial intelligence chips through third countries.
The Commerce Department on Monday moved to restrict exports of advanced AI chips to several Southeast Asian countries as part of measures aimed at curbing the transfer of the technology to China.
Washington already prohibits direct sales of its most advanced AI chips to China. However, Chinese companies have continued to access computing power by renting capacity at data centres in countries permitted to import the restricted chips.
The proposed tax on overseas data centre construction could further complicate this arrangement while pushing American companies to expand their infrastructure within the US.

Indian man sentenced to 19 years in US Sikh separatist assassination plot
Nikhil Gupta jailed for conspiring to hire a hitman to kill New York-based Sikh leader, Gurpatwant Singh Pannun.
An Indian national has been sentenced to more than 19-and-a-half years in prison in the United States in a murder-for-hire plot targeting a prominent Sikh separatist leader living in New York City.
Nikhil Gupta, 55, pleaded guilty in February to three conspiracy charges for plotting to hire a hitman to assassinate Gurpatwant Singh Pannun, a US citizen, lawyer and vocal advocate for a sovereign Sikh state.
US District Judge Victor Marrero handed down the 235-month sentence at a federal court in Manhattan on Friday. Gupta faces deportation to India after completing his prison term.
Addressing the court on Friday, Gupta said he regretted straying from the nonviolent example set by Indian independence leader Mahatma Gandhi. “I’m sorry to Mr Pannun, I’m sorry to the communities I hurt, I’m sorry to my own family,” he said.
Prosecutors accused Gupta of conspiring with an Indian government official to kill Pannun, a dual US-Canadian citizen and lawyer for the US-based separatist group Sikhs for Justice, in New York. Pannun is also a proponent of independence for Punjab, the northern Indian state where Sikhism was founded.
Court documents showed that Gupta and the Indian government official, Vikash Yadav, arranged to have $15,000 in cash delivered to someone who could kill Pannun. But the person turned out to be an undercover law enforcement officer posing as a hitman.
Gupta was arrested in Prague and has been held without bail since his extradition to the US in June 2023. A plea agreement called for him to serve at least two decades in prison.
Yadav is also charged in the case but is not in US custody. It is unclear whether he has hired a defence lawyer.
India’s government has denied any involvement in the plot against Pannun, saying it was against government policy.
However, multiple alleged assassination plots against Sikh separatists have been uncovered in the US and Canada, testing relations with India. New Delhi denies involvement in the plots.
‘A foot soldier’
Prosecutors with the Manhattan US Attorney’s Office had recommended a sentence of about 24 years in prison for Gupta.
“This case cuts to the very core of American values,” prosecutor Ashley Nicolas said in court. “We don’t condone the use of violence to silence voices in this country, ever.”
Pannun was in court on Friday to see the sentence handed down. He described Gupta as “just a foot soldier acting at the behest” of Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi, a Hindu nationalist who has opposed the independence movement.
Pannun said the Modi government wanted him dead “because I lead the campaign openly, defy threats and intimidation”.
Pannun also told the court he would keep advocating for Sikh sovereignty.
“Self-determination for my people and my homeland, Punjab, is my lifetime goal,” he said.

global-economics-cf143d3c5d.headline: Signal blocks screenshots to stop AI agents from reading private chats

Updated - November 20, 2026  at 11:35 PM.
| 
         NEW YORK
     Encrypted messaging service Signal said on Friday it would restrict screenshots to stop AI agents from reading private chats on phones, warning that the tech industry's push to embed AI in consumer devices was eroding its ability to guarantee privacy.
Signal, widely regarded by privacy advocates as a leader in secure messaging, called its new protections "incomplete" and urged operating system providers Apple, Alphabet's Google and Microsoft to give app developers more concrete ways to block the agents from accessing sensitive data.
It also called on those companies to provide more information about how their agents function, so developers can assess what data the bots are accessing and adjust their systems accordingly.
The move reflects growing tension between privacy-focused apps and the biggest tech companies, which are racing to roll out AI agents designed to see what is on a user's screen and take actions based on it.
Signal identified as particularly worrisome the AI capabilities built directly into operating systems, like Apple's Siri AI and Google's Gemini Intelligence, because of how deeply they are integrated into people's devices.
Operating systems maintain the environment in which Signal and other applications must exist, the company said in a blog post authored by its president, Meredith Whittaker.
"Right now, these agentic AI integrations are changing this environment in a way that’s making it increasingly hostile to privacy. This is an existential threat to Signal, and our ability to responsibly uphold our mission," the post said.
To prevent agents from scanning Signal messages, the service is introducing new settings blocking screenshot access on people's phones and switching those restrictions on by default. Users will receive pop-up windows giving them options to disable the blocks when Signal detects screenshot attempts or efforts by an AI assistant to access the screen, depending on the device.
Signal similarly blocked Microsoft's Recall AI from taking screenshots on Windows last year. It said it was unable to reliably offer such protections on Apple's macOS.
Apple, Google and Microsoft did not immediately respond to requests for comment on Signal's post.
Agents that can take actions on behalf of users are billed as the next big wave of AI technology, capable of surfacing relevant information from across different apps and executing time-saving tasks like answering emails, booking appointments and making online purchases autonomously, without direct instructions.
However, that reach can get around the protections that apps like Signal build for themselves.
Reuters reported earlier this week that Meta's Muse agent was able to bypass its own official "Connector" tool to access Signal messages on both an Apple computer and a phone using Google's Android system. In both cases, Muse used broad operating system-level permissions granted during the app's initial setup to pull in the messages, leveraging those authorizations in ways a user might not anticipate.
On Apple's macOS, for instance, it used a combination of the computer’s accessibility and screenshot tools, repurposing settings Apple offers for people with disabilities to navigate over to Signal, take screenshots of chats there, extract text from those pictures and reproduce the messages inside the Muse app.
An operating system update from Apple this week effectively closed that specific pathway, but also introduced a new set of permissions aimed at agents that offers similar capabilities paired with additional user warnings.
Meta said in response to Reuters' reporting that agents need to see and interact with people’s computers in order to work on their behalf, and that Muse can access other apps only via permissions users explicitly grant.
Signal said that developers should have straightforward ways of opting their apps out of such data processing by AI assistants entirely, specifically mentioning screen reading, notifications and other file system access.
The service, owned by a non-profit foundation, promises its users a secure messaging experience by limiting the data it stores on its own servers, eschewing ads and offering end-to-end encryption, meaning it cannot access and read the conversations conducted on its app.
AI systems that scan people's screens can undermine those protections by pulling the messages out of Signal's secure environment and into whatever other servers the agent is using, it said in its post.

science-mind-f6e77b7161.headline: Quantum effect could reverse gravity and violate Einstein’s theory of relativity
science-mind-f6e77b7161.fulltext:
Flying in the face of Albert Einstein’s theory of gravity, quantum physics could turn the famous force repulsive instead of attractive – and we could soon test the idea in the lab.
A hallmark of gravity as we know it is that it pulls objects with mass together: gravity explains why the moon orbits Earth, and why an apple falls to the ground after detaching from the tree. While this is well established, there is still no agreement on how gravity works at scales dominated by quantum effects, and what quantum properties it may have.
Now, two research teams have independently found that quantum effects can make gravity act repulsively, pushing objects apart instead of pulling them together.
Advertisement
“Gravity is always attractive – this has been the cornerstone of gravity from Newton to Einstein,” says Pablo Saldanha at the Federal University of Minas Gerais in Brazil, who worked on one of the studies with Vlatko Vedral and Chiara Marletto, both at the University of Oxford. “Anti-gravity or repulsion: no one has seen that before,” says Sougato Bose at University College London, who co-authored the other study with Lev Vaidman at Tel Aviv University in Israel.
A key concept for both studies was that of a quantum superposition state. Consider a car driving down a city street. When it arrives at an intersection where one road forks into two, it can take either the left or the right branch. But a quantum car would have another option: to enter a superposition of taking the left road and also the right one, assuming a state where it is impossible to tell where the car is exactly without disturbing it.
Another quantum object, called a “probe”, moving along a path parallel to both the left and right road branches, would be gravitationally attracted to the car. In both new studies, the researchers mathematically modelled an analogous setup and used equations to show that this gravitational interaction would make the car and the probe inextricably connected through the link of quantum entanglement.
The two teams mathematically examined a scenario equivalent to the two roads – left and right – merging some time after they had split apart. At this point, a measurement taken by the probe can reveal how each of the paths shaped the superposed car’s quantum state.
Quantum mechanics is probabilistic. This means that if this experiment is repeated many times, the final state of the car won’t always be the same, but will follow some distribution of states instead, reflecting its capacity to follow a combination of the left and right branches. The researchers in both experiments found that if all but some specific states were then discarded after the measurement – a technique called post-selection, partly pioneered by Vaidman – then the probe should theoretically experience gravitational repulsion and be pushed away from the car in the experiment. “That repulsion, that going away [from the superposed object], is created at the time of the measurement,” says Bose.
Even Einstein’s theory of general relativity, which has for over a century proven to be an incredibly accurate description of gravity, doesn’t predict this kind of gravitational repulsion. “There is a measurement that will somehow conditionally give you repulsive gravitational force,” says Vedral. Confirmation that such a repulsive force occurs would demonstrate the quantum nature of gravity.
Because this measurement effect is inherently quantum, just like the possibility of a superposition state is, the scenario the two teams explored doesn’t have any non-quantum analogues. But it could still be tested in experiments.
Objects that can stay in a superposition state for the duration of an experiment would have to be very small, says Bose, and yet also still massive enough for gravity to make a difference to their behaviour. Bacterium-sized objects should do the trick. He and Vaidman calculated that the probe object at this scale would experience acceleration roughly smaller than a quadrillionth of gravitational acceleration on Earth. Vedral says that he and his colleagues are already working with experimentalists who specialise in unusually large quantum objects.
Tomasz Paterek at the University of Gdańsk in Poland says that the new idea is “brilliant”. Past studies explored making the force between electrons attractive, even though it is usually repulsive, through post-selection. But this is the first time that the same process has been shown to potentially reverse gravity’s character too, he says. In Paterek’s view, lab experiments that use gravity to quantum entangle objects could be achievable in the near future – but he cautions they will be really difficult to perform.

Big Pharma Says AI and Anthropic Tools Shrink Preclinical Drug Discovery Timelines
Major pharmaceutical firms report artificial intelligence and Anthropic tools have cut preclinical drug discovery timelines by as much as fifty percent.
Published 20 Nov 2026· Last updated 20 Nov 2026· 7 minute read
On November 20, 2026, research executives across major pharmaceutical firms—including Novartis, AstraZeneca, GSK, and Sanofi—reported that generative artificial intelligence and Anthropic tools are compressing preclinical drug discovery timelines by up to 50 percent. Following earlier partnerships like the Merck-Isomorphic Labs oncology alliance, the acceleration shifts primary development bottlenecks to clinical trial execution and regulatory review, reshaping how academic translational centers and tech transfer offices structure discovery pipelines.
Preclinical Timelines Cut in Half Across Major Discovery Pipelines
Scientists and executives from leading drugmakers confirmed on November 20, 2026, that artificial intelligence has rapidly accelerated early-stage drug development over the past year. In disclosures detailed in Reuters investigative reporting and corroborated by syndicated reporting, drugmakers stated that algorithmic models have cut by as much as half the time required to design novel molecules, evaluate targets, and advance candidate therapies toward clinical trials.
The participating firms—comprising GSK, Bristol Myers Squibb, Novartis, Eli Lilly, Novo Nordisk, AstraZeneca, and Sanofi—emphasized that machine learning has moved beyond administrative filings. Today, computational models are embedded in core scientific workflows, including de novo molecular design, lead optimization, and toxicological screening.
“There is no part of the discovery through development pipeline where we are not using AI,” said Sharon Barr, executive vice president of biopharmaceuticals R&D at AstraZeneca. R&D leaders noted that while traditional discovery required years of wet-lab trial and error, modern neural architectures allow teams to screen vast chemical libraries and evaluate protein-ligand binding affinities in days.
Concrete Timeline Reductions and Model Deployments
Preclinical research groups shared quantitative milestones illustrating timeline compression across global pipelines:
Sanofi: Saved at least a full year developing its investigational asthma drug lunsekimig. By deploying machine learning to translate early biological findings into clinical decisions, the team bypassed an intermediate dose-selection trial stage entirely.
Novartis: Identified and prioritized five novel disease targets for its nephrology pipeline using AI screening tools, reducing project-initiation-to-candidate-selection time from three years down to 18 to 24 months.
Novo Nordisk: Reduced iterative design-make-test-analyze (DMTA) cycles from eight cycles to three. Automation slashed individual cycle durations from eight weeks to four weeks, shrinking lead optimization from 64 weeks to 12 weeks.
Bristol Myers Squibb: Chief Research Officer Robert Plenge confirmed that an investigational sickle cell anemia candidate advancing through its pipeline would not have been identified without internal AI systems, noting ongoing integration with laboratory robotics.
The table below summarizes preclinical timeline reductions, therapeutic focus areas, and AI deployment modes reported across major pharmaceutical organizations:
Frontier AI Moves From Software Provider to Biological Competitor
The acceleration of pharmaceutical pipelines coincides with expansions by frontier AI developers into biological discovery. Frontier laboratories are moving past software licensing to operate internal laboratories, creating a relationship pharmaceutical executives describe as coopetition.
Anthropic has deepened its life-sciences footprint through enterprise offerings and laboratory investments. In September 2026, the company launched its Life Sciences Verification Program to provide vetted pharmaceutical and academic teams secure access to frontier models with biology-specific safeguards. Alongside its Claude Science workbench, Anthropic established a San Francisco wet laboratory to validate AI-generated predictions empirically.
Institutional ties have also formalized: Novartis CEO Vas Narasimhan serves on Anthropic’s board of directors, bridging traditional pharmaceutical governance with computational intelligence. Anthropic also acquired startups Mithril Medicine and Coefficient Bio to seed an internal discovery pipeline targeting rare genetic disorders like muscular dystrophy.
At a Nasdaq address marking the company’s public valuation, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei stated that while biological experiments and clinical validation require time, AI models can substantially compress development schedules so fewer patients miss life-saving therapies. Additional industry analysis highlights that venture firms observe frontier AI laboratories pursuing biopharma acquisitions to acquire proprietary experimental datasets and laboratory infrastructure.
Clinical Trial Realities and the Human Validation Bottleneck
Despite efficiency gains in computational design and benchtop screening, industry scientists caution that early discovery represents only the initial phase of drug development. According to benchmark data from the Pharmaceutical Research and Manufacturers of America (PhRMA), developing a commercial medicine averages 10 to 15 years, requires billions of dollars in capitalized investment, and faces an overall clinical failure rate near 90 percent.
Pharmaceutical leaders also tempered expectations. Aliza Apple, who directs Eli Lilly’s TuneLab platform sharing internal models with biotechs, emphasized that claims of AI quickly curing all disease outpace scientific reality, noting tools must first deliver verifiable cures in specific indications.
The empirical realities of clinical translation were reinforced by a study published in Cancer Treatment Reviews by Dr. Waqas Haque, an oncology researcher at the University of Chicago, and colleagues. The team tracked the clinical pipeline of AI-enabled drugs, identifying 129 active therapeutic assets originating from 69 distinct companies entering human clinical trials as of 2026. However, the study revealed that the pipeline remains heavily early-stage: 57.3 percent (74 assets) are concentrated in oncology, only 24 assets (18.9 percent) have completed Phase 2 testing, and just 5 assets have advanced to Phase 3.
Dr. Haque emphasized that while preclinical candidate volume will surge, AI therapies face identical clinical hurdles. Human trial execution cannot be simulated away: patient recruitment, safety windows, and regulatory oversight under clinical trial transparency standards and clinical trial site SOPs remain fixed boundaries. Furthermore, surrogate computational endpoints require clinical proof under standards for digital biomarkers and digital endpoints in clinical trials.
Implications for Academic Medical Centers and Research Offices
The compression of preclinical timelines creates operational, legal, and strategic implications for university technology transfer offices, academic medical centers, and institutional sponsored programs offices:
Academic Translational Medicine Centers: University laboratories that spent years performing chemical lead optimization can now utilize foundation models to evaluate target candidates in months. This technological shift places a premium on wet-lab biological validation, patient-derived organoid assays, and translational models. Academic investigators benchmarking translational workflows frequently engage literature published in venues like the Journal of Clinical and Translational Science to align preclinical protocols with institutional standards.
Technology Transfer and Licensing Valuations: As AI tools lower the barrier to early molecular design, unoptimized academic targets command lower upfront licensing valuations from biopharma partners. To maximize institutional equity and royalty rights, university research offices are encouraging faculty to advance computational leads into preliminary in vitro or animal validation stages before initiating commercial licensing discussions.
Data Rights and IP Governance in Biopharma Contracts: University contracting offices must establish clear IP rules when faculty use external AI workbenches. Sponsored agreements must delineate ownership of downstream chemical derivatives and model weights trained on institutional cohorts. In clinical testing, academic teams structure agreements using templates like the model clinical trial agreement to protect data rights.
Next Milestones for Preclinical AI and Clinical Readouts
The biopharmaceutical industry and academic research community are monitoring several critical milestones through 2027 that will determine whether preclinical timeline compression translates into successful clinical therapies:
Phase 2 and 3 Oncology Readouts: Between late 2026 and mid-2027, the initial cohort of clinical-stage molecules designed with generative AI will report pivotal Phase 2 efficacy data, providing the first definitive test of whether computational design reduces historical Phase 2 attrition.
Regulatory Filings for AI-Optimized Leads: Global sponsors including Sanofi and Novartis plan to submit Investigational New Drug (IND) dossiers to the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) and European Medicines Agency (EMA) for candidate molecules whose preclinical development was compressed under 24 months.
Closed-Loop Robotic Automation Deployments: Throughout 2027, pharmaceutical facilities will complete direct integrations between generative AI algorithms and automated wet-lab robotics, establishing closed-loop systems that design, synthesize, and screen molecular leads with minimal manual intervention.
Academic Technology Transfer Standards: The Association of University Technology Managers (AUTM) is slated to release model contract terms in early 2027 addressing the licensing of foundational AI outputs, derivative molecular IP, and academic data contributions to commercial foundation models.

Trump threatens massive tax on US tech firms building data centres overseas
Donald Trump threatened a heavy tax on American technology companies building AI data centres overseas. The announcement, however, appeared to catch even his own administration off guard. Trump admitted that he had not yet discussed the proposal with his officials,
US President Donald Trump has threatened to impose a "tremendous tax" on American technology companies that build artificial intelligence data centres outside the country, in a fresh push to keep critical AI infrastructure on US soil to maintain its lead over China.
"We're not going to allow our companies to build data centres outside of our country," Trump said on Friday during a White House press briefing following his trip to Asia. He warned that companies choosing to construct such facilities overseas would face heavy financial penalties, although he offered no details about how the proposed tax would work.
The announcement, however, appeared to catch even his own administration off guard. Trump admitted that he had not yet discussed the proposal with his officials, leaving questions over whether the government would seek congressional approval or attempt to use existing executive powers to enforce the measure.
WHY TRUMP WANTS DATA CENTRES TO STAY IN THE US
Data centres are the backbone of the artificial intelligence revolution. These enormous facilities house thousands of computer servers that store information and provide the computing power required to train and operate advanced AI systems. Building such infrastructure has become increasingly important as companies race to develop more sophisticated artificial intelligence models. However, their construction is expensive and requires enormous amounts of electricity, water and land.
Trump has repeatedly backed the expansion of data centres in the United States, arguing that the infrastructure will strengthen the country's technological leadership and economic growth.
On Friday, he also said that American communities should welcome these projects rather than oppose them, urging residents and local authorities to negotiate better financial arrangements with developers.
"You ought to take advantage of the data centres," Trump said. "Make them pay you, make them pay your community, but don't shut them off."
"They're making so much money they don't know what to do with it," he added, arguing that communities should benefit financially from the investments.
However, the US President's proposal to penalise overseas construction could complicate the business plans of American data centre operators. Companies often establish facilities closer to their customers to reduce delays in data transmission, particularly for services such as financial transactions and other time-sensitive operations. Operating data centres in different countries can also help companies comply with local laws requiring certain information to be stored or processed within specific jurisdictions.
TRUMP'S CHINA CONCERNS AND THE AI RACE
Trump's remarks also carried a broader geopolitical message, with the President repeatedly framing the expansion of American AI infrastructure as essential to competing with China.
"We're not allowing data centres to go into other countries because China will take all of them, and we're not allowing that to happen," he said.
Washington has been tightening restrictions aimed at preventing Beijing from gaining access to advanced American computing technology. The Commerce Department on Monday announced new restrictions on remote access to advanced US computing chips and servers. The move is part of a wider effort to prevent Chinese companies from using computing capacity located in third countries to train sophisticated artificial intelligence models.
Although the US already restricts direct sales of its most advanced AI chips to China, Chinese companies have continued to find ways to access computing power through data centres in countries permitted to import the technology.
The latest restrictions seek to close some of these loopholes by limiting access to American computing infrastructure beyond US borders. Interestingly, Trump also spoke about the possibility of cooperation with China on artificial intelligence, despite his warnings about Beijing's technological ambitions.
He said he and Chinese President Xi Jinping had agreed to establish "some joint guardrails" for artificial intelligence, which Trump frequently describes as "superintelligence".
The US President maintained that Washington and Beijing were leading the global AI race, with "nobody even close", while stressing that the United States must emerge as the winner.
Trump also claimed that Xi respected and congratulated the US for its achievements in artificial intelligence.
AI BOOM MEETS LOCAL OPPOSITION
Trump's push for more data centre construction comes against the backdrop of growing resistance to these projects across the United States. Although technology companies have presented artificial intelligence as a major economic opportunity, communities have increasingly raised concerns about the environmental and financial costs of hosting large server facilities.
The biggest concerns centre on electricity consumption, pressure on local power infrastructure, rising utility bills, water requirements and the impact of construction on surrounding communities.
The issue also became a political flashpoint during the November midterm elections, with several Democratic candidates promising tougher oversight of data centre development.
According to figures cited by Axios, voters favoured restrictions on data centre development in 52 of 53 ballot measures across 13 states through November 2026. The issue also provided Democratic challengers with an opportunity to target Republicans over their approach to artificial intelligence infrastructure.
The growing opposition has forced technology giants to reconsider how they approach communities where they want to build. Companies including Google and Meta have been trying to address public mistrust by offering greater transparency, increasing financial incentives and promising to reduce the environmental impact of their facilities.
They have also sought to reassure residents that data centre investments can benefit local economies, including through improvements in property values.

Updated - November 20, 2026  at 10:04 PM.
Dario Amodei may have rung the ceremonial bell after Anthropic’s record-breaking IPO late on Thursday evening, but Indian retail investors have woken up to one of the hottest tech stocks on the market.
Anthropic’s scrip, which began trading on Nasdaq at $111.50 per share (roughly ₹10,400) quickly climbed the ranks to become one of the highest-traded stocks on specialised investment platforms that allow Indians to trade in global stocks.
The AI company accounted for about 11 per cent of all traded value on investment platform Vested, while 9 per cent of all trades (in volume terms) was for Anthropic buy orders.
Vested said that the average buy order for Anthropic stood at $1,100 or roughly ₹1 lakh while 20 per cent of the active traders on Thursday’s session bought the scrip. About 84% of the trades were placed just two hours after the scrip began trading.
Viram Shah, Founder and CEO, Vested said that Anthropic attracted considerable interest among Indian investors because it offered direct exposure to the AI models and applications rather than just the semiconductor and infrastructure companies powering them.
Vested did not share absolute value of investments in Anthropic. Vested’s last reported customer assets as of June stands at ₹15,000 crore across 5 lakh accounts with 80 per cent of this is held in US public markets.
Indmoney, another company that offers US stock investing, said that investors on its platform placed bids for Anthropic that are 2X higher than average. The company said that 40 per cent of all our order volume on Thursday was for Anthropic. Indmoney’s global assets under management, as per previous reporting, is around $3.5 billion.
Anthropic shares closed after its first session at $97.17, up $14.17 or 17.07 per cent from its listing price.
Naresh Biyani, Founder & CEO of Capwise Financial Service said that early price moves will reflect flows more than fundamentals with the real test coming after first quarterly results and the lock-in expiry.
As for other stocks that dominated trade on Vested, chip major AMD, whose shares have been tanking after reports spotlighting its business with China, saw high trading activity. Its rival Nvidia, embroiled in controversies of its own, came in third.
